lead: Solidity is a statically typed language for writing smart contracts on Ethereum. A compiler turns a .sol file into EVM bytecode. The language exists so a developer can name state, functions, events and access rules in one contract. It is used for tokens, wallets, DeFi pools, NFT marketplaces and DAO voting. This chapter reads a small contract line by line: pragma, state, mapping, functions, visibility, modifiers, events, errors, payable, inheritance and storage versus memory. Some syllabi call this the Solidity language or smart contract programming.
prereq: You need: 5.3 EVM for bytecode and gas, and 5.4 contract lifecycle for what a contract account is.

blocks.text: Every Solidity file starts with a version pragma. pragma solidity ^0.8.0; means compile with a 0.8.x compiler, not 0.7.x. Compiler versions differ, so the pragma pins the rules the file expects. A contract is a type: it holds state variables and functions at one address.

contract declares the type. mapping(address => uint) is a hash table from an account address to an unsigned integer. address is a 20-byte Ethereum account identifier. uint means uint256, a non-negative integer from 0 to 2²⁵⁶−1. balances is a state variable: it lives in contract storage on every node. public makes Solidity generate a getter function called balances(address); it does not make the variable callable as balances(). An unknown key returns 0, because every storage slot starts at zero. That zero default is useful and dangerous: it looks like a real balance of zero, never an error.
A function declares inputs, visibility, mutability and output.

function starts the definition. deposit is the name. public means callable from outside and inside the contract. payable allows ether with the call. msg.sender is the caller address. msg.value is the wei sent; 1 ETH = 10¹⁸ wei. += adds to the stored balance. emit Paid(...) writes a log.

Visibility: public callable anywhere; external only from outside; internal only this contract and children; private only this contract. view promises no state change; pure promises no state read or change.

A modifier wraps a function with a check. modifier positive(uint x) { require(x > 0, "zero"); _; } The underscore _ is where the function body runs. require(condition, message) reverts the whole call if false. Modern code can use error ZeroAmount(); then revert ZeroAmount();; a custom error is cheaper than a string.
An event is a log declaration: event Paid(address indexed who, uint amount); indexed makes a searchable topic. Events are not readable by contracts; they are for off-chain tools.

storage is permanent state on chain. memory is temporary data for one call. A local variable of a reference type, such as a string or array, must say where it lives. string memory name = "Asha"; is copied for the call. Assigning a storage pointer to a memory variable copies; assigning storage to storage shares. Value types like uint and address are copied by default.

Inheritance lets a contract reuse code: contract Savings is SimpleBank { ... } Savings gets the state and functions of SimpleBank. A child can override a function marked virtual by marking its own override. Constructor code runs once at deployment. address payable is an address that can receive ether with transfer or send; plain address cannot. In 0.8.x, arithmetic overflow reverts by default, so x + y on uint is checked.

examples.question: A contract SimpleBank has mapping(address => uint) balances. Alice deposits 0.5 ETH, Bob deposits 0.2 ETH, and Alice withdraws 0.1 ETH. Give Alice balance, Bob balance and total contract balance.
steps: Start: Alice = 0 ETH, Bob = 0 ETH, contract total = 0 ETH.
Alice deposits 0.5 ETH: Alice = 0.5 ETH, Bob = 0 ETH, contract total = 0.5 ETH.
Bob deposits 0.2 ETH: Alice = 0.5 ETH, Bob = 0.2 ETH, contract total = 0.7 ETH.
Alice withdraws 0.1 ETH: Alice = 0.5 − 0.1 = 0.4 ETH, Bob stays 0.2 ETH, contract total = 0.4 + 0.2 = 0.6 ETH.
examples.answer: Alice = 0.4 ETH; Bob = 0.2 ETH; contract total = 0.6 ETH.
examples.check:
alice = 0.5 - 0.1
bob = 0.2
total = alice + bob
print(round(alice, 10))
print(round(bob, 10))
print(round(total, 10))
examples.output:
Alice 0.4 ETH
Bob 0.2 ETH
contract total 0.6 ETH

traps: A mapping returns 0 for an unknown key; it does not revert. A zero balance and a missing key look the same.
address and address payable are not the same; only address payable can be the target of transfer.
A public state variable creates a getter function; balances is storage, balances(addr) is a call.
memory is a copy for one call; storage is the permanent value. Writing to a memory copy does not change the chain.
require(false) reverts state and returns unused gas; it does not return the gas already paid. A revert undoes state changes.

quiz.a: Compile this file with a 0.8.x Solidity compiler; the caret allows later 0.8 releases but not 0.7 or 0.9.

quiz.q: Why does mapping(address => uint) return 0 for an address never seen?
quiz.a: Every storage slot starts at zero. A mapping does not store a list of keys, so an unknown key reads the zero default.

quiz.q: A contract has mapping(address => uint) balances. Alice deposits 0.3 ETH; Bob deposits 0.1 ETH; Alice withdraws 0.2 ETH. Give Alice balance, Bob balance and contract total.
quiz.a: Alice = 0.3 − 0.2 = 0.1 ETH; Bob = 0.1 ETH; contract total = 0.1 + 0.1 = 0.2 ETH.

quiz.q: Why is public balances not the same as a function that lets any user set any balance?
quiz.a: public on a state variable only generates a read-only getter. It does not create a setter. Writing requires a function with its own visibility and checks.

quiz.q: What does payable enable on a function?
quiz.a: It allows the function call to carry ether, read as msg.value in wei.

quiz.q: How many wei are in 1 ETH?
Why use a modifier instead of repeating the same require in every function?
quiz.a: A modifier names one check in one place. Every function that uses it runs the same rule before its body, so the contract is shorter and less likely to miss a check.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production Solidity now uses custom errors, checked arithmetic by default in 0.8.x, and gas-aware patterns in ERC-20 and ERC-721 contracts. OpenZeppelin provides audited base contracts for tokens and access control. Foundry and Hardhat are common build and test tools; Slither is a static analyzer. Search for Solidity custom errors, ERC-20, OpenZeppelin, Foundry and Slither to go further.
